# Provenance of the engine configuration goldens

Same discipline as `internal/netcfg/testdata/PROVENANCE.md`. A fixture nobody
can trace is a fixture whose class nobody can tell, so it silently becomes
evidence it is not.

`test/goldenscan`'s `TestEveryTestdataDirectoryHasAProvenanceFile` requires this
file. It was added on 2026-08-30, after the directory had gone without one. The
entries for the files that predate it are written from `golden_test.go` and
`fixtures_test.go`, which are their record; that is second-hand and is marked
where it matters.

## Class of every file here

GENERATED. Every `.json` file is the output of `Build` or `BuildFailClosed` in
this package, from an invented share link. Nothing here came from a running
system, a real account, or a real server.

## What a green run here proves, and what it does not

More than most golden directories, and it is worth being exact about which part
is which.

- `TestGolden` proves the bytes have not changed.
- `TestGoldenFilesAreAcceptedByTheEngine` proves more: it reads the COMMITTED
  files, not freshly generated bytes, and puts each one through
  `engine.Validate`. An engine upgrade can invalidate a document without a line
  of this package changing, and without this the golden test would stay green
  while the box would not start.
- Neither proves the document does what it claims once running. That is the
  hardware harness's question and the live-transport question, not this one.

## How to regenerate

    bash scripts/golden-update.sh

or this package alone:

    go test ./internal/xcfg -run Golden -update

Then READ THE DIFF, and read it for the three things a struct literal hides:
which outbound is FIRST, what order the routing rules are in, and which key the
resolver list is under.

## Credentials

These documents ARE credential-carrying documents. That is what an engine
configuration is for: it holds the user id, the REALITY public key, the short
id, the password or the auth string, and the server address. There is nothing to
redact here without destroying the thing being pinned.

What makes that safe is that every input is invented. The share links are built
in `internal/xcfg/fixtures_test.go` out of their parts rather than pasted as one
string, so a reader can see at a glance that they are fake, and that file says so
in its own header. The values are:

    fakeUUID            11111111-2222-4333-8444-555555555555, a syntactically
                        valid UUID and nobody's account
    fakePublicKey()     base64 of the ASCII text CASPIAN-FAKE-REALITY-PUBKEY-3232,
                        which is 32 bytes because that is what the engine requires
    fakeMldsa65Verify() the same trick repeated to 1952 bytes
    fakeShortID         ten hexadecimal characters
    fakeHost            example.invalid, which RFC 2606 reserves and which
                        therefore resolves nowhere
    fakeSNI             www.fake-front.invalid, likewise

`test/goldenscan` allowlists the `uuid`, `base64-32byte-key` and `routable-ipv4`
classes for `internal/xcfg/testdata/*.json` on exactly those grounds, and each
allowlist entry names the fixture function so the claim can be checked rather
than taken.

The routable addresses in these documents are the public resolvers this
repository chooses in `resolvers.go`: Quad9 at 9.9.9.9 and 9.9.9.11, Cloudflare
at 1.1.1.3, CleanBrowsing at 185.228.168.9. They are identical on every box and
identify nobody.

## Every file

### The reference document and the option axes, predating 2026-08-30

    reality-default.json                a REALITY link with nothing overridden. Read
                                        this one first when reviewing a change
    reality-intercept.json              the DNS interception switch on. Note in the
                                        diff that the resolver rule stays ABOVE the
                                        port 53 rule
    reality-localdns.json               the loopback DNS listener alone, which is what
                                        makes internal/hotspot's dnsmasq able to
                                        resolve anything. The local DNS rule and the
                                        resolver rule are both ABOVE private-direct,
                                        and that is what stops a query being answered
                                        on the local network
    reality-localdns-and-intercept.json both switches, so it is visible that they are
                                        separate rules and not one mechanism with two
                                        names
    reality-socks-only.json             no TUN inbound. This is the document
                                        docs/2026-08-29-design.md section 8 step 4
                                        describes, used to capture an exit IP before
                                        any addressing exists
    reality-everything-overridden.json  every option moved off its default at once, so
                                        a change to a default shows in one file and a
                                        change to the SHAPE shows in all of them

`TestEveryOptionsFieldIsOverriddenInTheGolden` keeps the last one honest. It
failed for real once: `LocalDNS` was added to `Options` and not to the case, and
the file still generated, still validated and still matched itself while covering
one fewer field than its name claims.

### One per protocol shape

    vless-tls-ws.json   predates 2026-08-30
    vmess-ws-tls.json   predates 2026-08-30
    shadowsocks.json    predates 2026-08-30
    trojan.json         predates 2026-08-30
    hysteria2.json      predates 2026-08-30
    socks.json          ADDED 2026-08-30
    hy2-alias.json      ADDED 2026-08-30

The last two closed a measured gap rather than a suspected one.
`internal/link/link.go`'s `supportedSchemes` declares seven schemes: vless,
vmess, ss, socks, trojan, hysteria2 and hy2. `goldenCases()` froze five protocol
shapes and left two with no golden at all. Probed on 2026-08-30:

    the socks scheme  link.Parse accepts it, Build produces a 2036 byte
                      document, and no test in this package had ever looked at it
    the hy2 scheme    parses to protocol "hysteria", the same as hysteria2

(The two scheme names are written in words rather than as URIs on purpose:
test/goldenscan reports a share-link shape in any committed fixture, and a
provenance file that reproduces the shape it is explaining trains people to
allowlist the class.)

`socks` is a genuinely distinct outbound protocol that nothing had reviewed.
`hy2` is worth a file precisely BECAUSE it is supposed to be an alias: if the two
documents ever stop agreeing, a user who pasted the short form gets a different
outbound from a user who pasted the long one, and the only symptom is that one of
them does not connect. `TestGolden_Hy2AndHysteria2ProduceTheSameOutbound`
compares the outbound sections directly and says that in its failure message.

`TestGolden_EverySupportedSchemeHasAGolden` now fails when an eighth scheme is
added to `internal/link` without a golden, so this gap cannot reopen quietly.

### The fail-closed document

    fail-closed.json

`BuildFailClosed`. Its whole content is the claim that there is no way out of it,
which is why it gets a file of its own. `document-shape.txt` shows the claim at a
glance: it has exactly ONE outbound, `protocol=blackhole tag=block`, where every
other document has three.

### The shape summary, added 2026-08-30

    document-shape.txt

The top-level keys, the inbound tags in order, and the outbound protocols and
tags IN ORDER, for every transport plus the fail-closed document.

Outbound order is load-bearing and this is the file that makes it readable. The
FIRST outbound is where anything the routing rules do not match goes, so a
protocol arriving at position 0 is a change in the default route for unmatched
traffic. In a diff of a 6000 byte JSON document that is invisible unless somebody
is hunting for it; here it is one line.
